---
title: "Counterbalancing"
---

Suppose an acceptability study compares active and passive descriptions in matched discourse contexts. The linguistic question is whether the voice alternation changes acceptability under those contexts. Showing both versions of one lexical item to the same participant may reveal the manipulation or create repetition effects. Showing only one version avoids that problem, but it creates another: if every participant sees item A only in the active condition, any special property of item A is inseparable from voice.

[**Counterbalancing**](https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/) distributes item versions across stimulus lists so that each participant sees an item only once, while each item occurs in every condition across participants. Basically, conditions change within an item across the complete set of lists, not within one participant's session. This is the **item-rotation principle** (IRP).

## Representing the design as a condition map

Let $C_{jl}$ denote the condition assigned to item $j$ in list $l$. For a two condition design with two lists, a complete counterbalance requires

$$
\{C_{j1},C_{j2}\}=\{0,1\}
$$

for every item $j$. Each item must appear once in condition 0 and once in condition 1 across the two lists. Within each list, condition counts should also be balanced so that a participant encounters both conditions equally often.

The equation constrains the mapping from items to lists. Participant assignment to lists is a separate draw governed by the [random assignment mechanism](random-assignment.qmd) introduced earlier.

## Constructing a two list design by hand

Consider four sentence items and two conditions.

| item | list 1 | list 2 |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | active | passive |
| B | passive | active |
| C | active | passive |
| D | passive | active |

Read the table in two directions. Down list 1, there are two active and two passive items. The same is true of list 2. Across the row for item A, both conditions occur. The same is true for B, C, and D. The column check balances what one participant sees; the row check implements the IRP.

This structure separates item identity from condition across lists. If item A is unusually acceptable because of its lexical content or discourse context, that tendency contributes to the active condition in list 1 and the passive condition in list 2. Thus, item A is not permanently attached to one condition.

The condition map can be generated and checked in R.

```{r}
counterbalance <- data.frame(
  item = rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = 2),
  list = rep(c("list_1", "list_2"), times = 4),
  condition = c(
    "active", "passive",
    "passive", "active",
    "active", "passive",
    "passive", "active"
  )
)

with(counterbalance, table(item, condition))
with(counterbalance, table(list, condition))
```

The first table checks that every item appears in both conditions across lists. The second checks that each list contains equal condition counts. These are different margins of the design. Neither table checks trial order, discourse-context balance, or whether the active and passive versions preserve the intended propositional content; those require separate stimulus checks.

## Lists must reach participants by design

A valid condition map can still be undermined by how lists are distributed. Suppose list 1 is used during the first week and list 2 during the second. Testing week, recruitment source, or experimenter experience may then become associated with list. Because item conditions change with list, those properties may also become associated with condition.

Participants should thus be randomly assigned to lists or assigned through a recorded restricted mechanism that balances list counts. The realized assignment should be checked after missed sessions and exclusions. Planned balance does not imply realized balance.

## Counterbalancing does not remove dependence

Each participant still supplies several ratings, and each item is still rated by several participants. Counterbalancing makes the within-item condition contrast available across lists. It does not make the rows independent, eliminate participant and item variation, or turn an acceptability contrast into a direct measure of grammaticality.

Averaging over a perfectly balanced table can hide heterogeneous effects. An item may respond differently to the manipulation, and a participant may be more sensitive to the contrast. The [random slope models introduced earlier](../regression-models/random-slopes.qmd) can represent variation in the condition contrast across repeated units, but the model still depends on the counterbalanced design for an interpretable comparison.

## More than two factors

Several factors can require more lists. If two binary manipulations are fully crossed, each item has four possible versions. A complete rotation distributes all four versions across lists while showing only one version of an item to each participant.

Using only part of the crossing is possible, but omitted combinations impose assumptions about which effects can be separated. Before collection, write the item-by-list condition map and verify that every planned contrast changes within items across the complete design. A Latin square is one construction for rotating conditions; the name does not by itself guarantee balanced list counts, appropriate order, or an estimable linguistic contrast.

## Checking balance after data collection

A design can be balanced in its plan but unbalanced in its collected observations. Missing sessions, programming errors, or unequal exclusions can produce this discrepancy. After collection, tabulate item by condition, list by condition, and participant by condition using the retained observations.

A second failure occurs when a condition is permanently attached to an item. No amount of participant balance can then distinguish the condition effect from the item. This failure must be repaired in the stimulus lists, not in the fitted model.

::: {.callout-note title="Audit the counterbalance"}
1. Which table margin checks that every item appears in every condition?
2. Which table margin checks that a participant assigned to one list encounters balanced condition counts?
3. Why can assigning list 1 before list 2 confound list with testing time?
4. Does perfect counterbalancing make repeated responses independent?
:::

Counterbalancing distributes item versions so that condition can vary within items across the complete design without repeating an item within a participant. The realized data must preserve both the item margin and the list margin.
